passage:
Sunday night, last day of first year.

Marks are down again. Seema asked me over tea why I don't just change courses. I said, "Papa has paid the fees, how can I waste that?" She looked at me and didn't argue. I hate the lectures. I dread the labs. But I'm Papa's only son, and the whole family tells everyone I'm going to be an engineer. What would they say?

I keep telling myself another year, then it will click. It didn't click this year. I've stopped drawing, which I used to love. I don't know how to tell anyone that fees paid isn't the same as a life chosen.

Sahil

qa.q: What did Sahil tell Seema about the fees?
qa.a: Sahil said that Papa has paid the fees and asked how it could be wasted.

qa.q: Why does Sahil keep going on the course although the lectures and labs feel dreadful?
qa.a: Sahil feels trapped between money already paid and the family's pride, and fears the judgement if he leaves.

qa.q: What could Sahil do differently, and why?
qa.a: Sahil could talk with Papa or a counsellor about a change of course, because fees already paid cannot be recovered but the coming years can still be chosen.

qa.q: How might Seema see Sahil's reasoning about the fees?
qa.a: Seema listens quietly and seems to sense that paid fees are not the real reason, so she may be worried about him.

grounding: A student in a disliked course keeps going, citing fees already paid and family expectations, staying in a poor fit for a year.

passage:
In the small town of Rahatgaon, everyone knew Vijay was the first in his family to join the polytechnic. When his cousin Zeenat asked him at the temple fair how civil engineering was, he said, "Fine."
It wasn't. He had wanted electronics, but the civil seat came first, and his father had borrowed from a neighbour for the fees. Every time Vijay thought of switching, he pictured the neighbour at the tea stall asking why.
So he stayed. He copied site-survey notes from friends, failed a surveying practical, and spent his evenings fixing radios for people in the lane, which was the only part of his day he enjoyed.
By the end of the year, Zeenat noticed he had stopped mentioning college at all. "You fix radios better than anyone here," she said. Vijay looked at the soldering iron and didn't answer.

qa.q: What did Vijay fix in the evenings?
qa.a: He fixed radios for people in the lane.

qa.q: What does Vijay's silence at the end suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels trapped and sad, knowing the radios are what he enjoys but afraid to admit the course is wrong for him.

qa.q: What else could Vijay have done in his first term?
qa.a: He could have asked the polytechnic about switching to electronics and talked honestly with his father, since fear of the neighbour's questions was costing him a year.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see what is happening to Vijay?
qa.a: Zeenat notices he has stopped talking about college and gently points to his real skill, showing she sees the poor fit.

grounding: Shows a student staying in a course he dislikes because of fees already paid and fear of what people will say, losing a year to a poor fit.
